newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Yeltsin joyful as prepares to sign Ukraine treaty.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin joyful as prepares to sign Ukraine treaty.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin arrived in Ukraine on Friday and said he was full of "joy and hope" at the prospect of ending years of arguing by the neighbouring Slav states over the Black Sea Fleet.
Both he and President Leonid Kuchma said they were sure a friendship treaty which has been held up by a row over the shareout of the former Soviet fleet would be signed on Saturday.

Yeltsin, who has cancelled at least six trips to sign the treaty, clearly relished the opportunity of playing the peacemaker and declared Ukraine should never lose the independence it won when the Soviet Union fell apart in 1991.
He took part of the blame for the fact that relations between the two most powerful Soviet states had been so tricky.
"Of course, probably we are also to blame. This must be put right," he said, adding: "I come with joy and hope."
The Russian leader swept aside the chief of his protocol department who tried to direct him into a waiting limousine after he stepped out of his plane.
Instead he strode determinedly up to a crowd of reporters to tell them he had a great feeling of excitement and hope.
Later he met Kuchma at his palace residence, announcing: "We will sign a string of documents which open huge possibilities for Russians and Ukrainians."
Kuchma shared his optimism, saying: "What we have been striving for, what we have been working for...will be completed tomorrow. And without exaggerating, I see this event as historic".

Yeltsin made clear he did not share the view of parliamentarians at home who have urged the Kremlin to question Ukraine's right to Crimea, the Russian-populated Black Sea region handed over from Russia to Ukraine in 1954.

"The main thing is that we are equal. The main thing is that we have no claims to any Ukrainian lands. This is a single Ukraine and it must be united and indivisible. I am convinced of this. It must be this way," Yeltsin said.
The two countries' prime ministers on Wednesday signed a deal leasing the Crimean port of Sevastopol to Russia for it to keep its lion's share of the Black Sea Fleet for 20 years.
But a hint of the divisions between Russia and Ukraine was felt on Friday despite the display of Slav brotherliness.

Ukraine, which is trying to free itself from centuries of Moscow domination by seeking strategic alliances elsewhere, said it had never sought a promise by Yeltsin before his arrival that Moscow would defend Ukraine "in extreme situations".

"I think President Yeltsin was ruled by his best intentions but there were no requests from the Ukrainian side," Volodymyr Horbulin, Secretary of Ukraine's policy-making Security and Defence Council, told a news conference.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told reporters in Kiev that Russia had not changed its negative view of plans for NATO-led naval exercises off Crimea in August.
"We see certain anti-Russian hints in these exercises," he said, referring to the "Sea-Breeze" exercises which will include the Ukrainian navy. Russia declined an invitation to take part.

Unlike Moscow, Kiev does not oppose plans by to admit new members in Eastern Europe and on Thursday initialled a pact with the Western defence alliance giving it the right to call for "consultations" if it feels under external threat.

On May 27 Yeltsin signed an agreement with NATO establishing a new security relationship but repeated his warning that Russia would rethink relations with the Western alliance if it sought to expand into the ex-Soviet republics.
Ukraine has never turned to Russia for security protection since it gained independence in 1991 and some circles in Kiev see Moscow as a threat rather than a brotherly Slav state.
